t: Erect the Fence II — Smallest Enclosing Circle via Welzl's Algorithm
o: We need the minimum-radius circle that covers every tree, returned as [x, y, r] with answers accepted within 10^-5. In Example 1 all six trees lie exactly on or inside the circle centered at (2,2) with radius 2. In Example 2 the three trees are covered by the circle centered at (2.5,2) with radius 1.5, whose diameter stretches between the extreme points. A classical geometric fact anchors every solution: the optimal circle is unique and is determined by either two antipodal boundary points (the diameter case) or three boundary points (their circumcircle). With up to 3000 trees, testing candidate circles naively is far too slow, so we use randomized incremental construction (Welzl), which processes points in random order and grows the circle only when forced.
k: The minimum enclosing circle is unique and always has two or three trees on its boundary — two forming a diameter, or three defining a circumcircle.
Welzl's algorithm processes points in random order; whenever a point lies outside the current circle, it must lie ON the boundary of every enclosing circle of the processed prefix.
Collinear triples make the circumcircle determinant vanish, so a fallback to the smallest covering pair-diameter is required for correctness.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate Boundary Pairs and Triples
a.i: Since the answer is defined by two or three boundary points, enumerate every diameter circle through a pair and every circumcircle through a triple, verify each candidate covers all trees, and keep the smallest radius. This is the clearest proof of correctness and instant on tiny inputs, but O(n^3) candidates times O(n) verification is hopeless at n = 3000 — it motivates the incremental algorithm.
s: For each ordered pair (i, j), form the diameter circle centered at their midpoint.
For each triple (i, j, k), form the circumcircle from the linear-system formula, skipping degenerate collinear triples.
Verify each candidate against every tree with an epsilon-tolerant containment test.
Track the smallest-radius candidate; default to the single-point circle of radius 0.
a.t: O(n^4) — O(n^3) candidate circles each verified against all n trees
a.sp: O(n) — the candidate list for one fixed pair

a.i: Shuffle the points, then grow the circle incrementally: when point P[i] falls outside the current circle, it must be on the final boundary, so rebuild a circle pinned to P[i] while rescanning earlier points; a violation there pins a second point P[j]; a further violation pins a third and takes their circumcircle. Random shuffling makes each restart trigger with probability at most 3/i, giving expected linear time even though the worst case stays cubic. Collinear triples are handled by falling back to the smallest pair-diameter covering the triple.
s: Shuffle the points uniformly at random.
For each i, skip points already inside the current circle; otherwise reset the circle to just point i.
Rescan j < i: on violation set the circle to the diameter of points i and j.
Rescan k < j: on violation set the circle to the circumcircle of i, j, k (pair-diameter fallback if collinear).
Return the final center and radius.
a.t: Expected O(n) — random shuffling bounds restart probability by 3/i per level; deterministic worst case O(n^3)
a.sp: O(1) — a handful of circles beyond the input copy

w: Open with the brute force to establish that two or three boundary points define the optimum, then implement Welzl as the production answer. Pitfalls: collinear triples yield a zero determinant and need the pair-diameter fallback; omitting the shuffle invites adversarial cubic behavior; containment checks require an epsilon since circumcenters come from floating-point solves (answers within 10^-5 are accepted); a lone tree returns radius 0. Mention that restricting candidates to convex-hull vertices also prunes work but does not beat expected-linear Welzl. Follow-up: smallest enclosing ball in higher dimensions generalizes the same recurrence, and axis-weighted variants lead to ellipses.
